title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust and the Dollar

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of one of the great novels of the Victorian age.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be moving through Charles Dickens's last completed novel — chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
It's a novel about money — about what it does to people, what people do for it, and what it costs them when they get it.
It's also one of the most atmospherically strange and morally serious things Dickens ever wrote.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the dust, the river, and the world Dickens builds around them.
Joining me are three readers whose company I very much value.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most elegant literary critics of his generation.
He reads novels as moral dramas — as tests of individual character — and he brings to this book a lifetime's knowledge of what makes fiction endure.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose work traces how institutions actually functioned in the Victorian world.
He knows what it meant to be poor in 1860s London — and he doesn't let Dickens, or us, look away from that.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager.
She's the reader in the room who will tell us what actually moves her — and why certain sentences refuse to leave you alone.
Let's begin with the world Dickens creates — its atmosphere, its moral texture, the strange light it casts on everyone who passes through it.
What strikes me, returning to this novel after many years, is how deliberately Dickens refuses to let you settle.
From the very opening — the river, the scavenging, the dead body being rowed through the dark — he places you inside a world that is morally suspended.
No one is quite what they appear to be.
The dust heaps are fortunes in disguise; the drowned man is an identity waiting to be shed.
Dickens had done dark before — but rarely with such sustained, architectural purpose.
Johnson, I think, would have recognised the moral seriousness beneath the grotesquerie.
Edmund is right that nothing is quite stable — and that instability is historically precise, not merely atmospheric.
The dust heaps were real — enormous mounds of household refuse on the outskirts of London, and the men who owned them were genuinely wealthy.
Old Harmon's fortune built on other people's rubbish — that wasn't a metaphor Dickens invented.
That was Victorian capitalism with the lid off.
And what I want us to keep in mind is how this world shapes everyone who moves through it — including the characters we're most inclined to admire.
Take a passage I've been thinking about — two young women alone of an evening, brushing each other's hair by firelight.
Dickens writes of Lizzie loosening Jenny Wren's hair, and then of Jenny doing the same for Lizzie in return.
He says the hair — Jenny's long fair hair —
Poor shoulders — that's a quietly devastating phrase.
The tenderness of that scene exists alongside the knowledge of Jenny's physical suffering — Dickens doesn't let you have the beauty without the pain.
That passage undoes me every time.
What Dickens is doing there — and it's very quietly done — is building an entire friendship out of small physical kindnesses.
These two women have almost nothing.
And what they give each other is attention — careful, unspoken, intimate attention.
The hair becomes almost a kind of language — darker and fairer, rich and poor, and yet the two women utterly at ease with one another.
It's one of the most genuinely gentle things in a novel that can be very savage.
And that contrast — the gentleness and the savagery — is precisely what I mean by Dickens's moral imagination.
He doesn't resolve it.
He places the firelit tenderness and the haggard menace in the same world and invites you to feel both at once.
And that menace, when it comes, is rendered with extraordinary compression.
There is a passage involving Bradley Headstone — that disturbed, obsessive schoolmaster — creeping up a dark staircase toward the chambers of Wrayburn and Lightwood.
Dickens describes him as a — and the phrase is extraordinary — as a 'haggard head' floating up the stairs.
And the narrator observes, with tremendous understatement:
The Gothic dread is entirely earned — and entirely restrained.
What strikes me about that Headstone passage is that it is also socially precise.
Headstone is a man of rigidly achieved respectability — a schoolmaster, a person of earned status — watching, from the dark, two men of effortless class who will never take him seriously.
His violence is born partly of that humiliation.
Which brings me to another pair — far less sympathetic — and to Dickens's most cold-eyed dismissal in the entire novel.
The Lammles — two frauds who married each other, each believing the other had money — are finally expelled from the novel.
Dickens watches them walk away down the long street — arm in arm, silent — and writes:
No rage, no melodrama.
They simply — cease.
That line about turning the street corner is one of the great quiet exits in Victorian fiction.
Dickens doesn't curse them.
He simply erases them — and there's something more damning in that than any denunciation.
What I love is that image of them walking arm-in-arm like respectable people — Dickens says they walked 'showily enough' — but in total, haggard silence.
The performance of marriage without a scrap of its substance.
The firelit tenderness, the haggard face on the staircase, the couple who walk out of the world — all in the same novel.
That breadth of register is, I think, what makes Our Mutual Friend so inexhaustible.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the characters at the centre of it all — and to the question of what this novel makes of goodness, and of the people who try to live by it.

segments.title: A Gentleman's Fall: John Harmon's Shadow

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We turn now to one of the novel's most elaborate constructions: the identity of John Harmon.
A man who is supposed to be dead, living under an assumed name, watching the life that should have been his.
And at the heart of this plot is a relationship — between Harmon and the Boffins — built on years of kindness that Harmon himself never witnessed firsthand.
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us from Oxford, bringing his unfailing attention to moral character and individual conscience.
Professor James Blackstone is here with the institutional and legal backdrop that makes the inheritance plot so consequential.
And Caroline Woodcourt, whose close readings of this novel have always found the human pulse beneath the mechanism.
Edmund, let's begin with the backstory — the Boffins as advocates for young John against his father's cruelty.
What strikes me most about that early revelation is the sheer moral weight Dickens places on two servants.
Boffin and his wife are not gentry. They have no formal claim on the boy. And yet they stand between him and a brutal old man, again and again.
Dickens renders this with a peculiarly vivid touch — Boffin recounts it to Mortimer Lightwood, and the detail of Mrs Boffin's bonnet is unforgettable.

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard.'
'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
That repetition — 'Dropped her' — is Dickens at his most surgical.
It is not sentiment. It is testimony. Boffin is a witness, and he wants the fact to land with its full force.
That passage always stops me cold on re-reading.
The black straw bonnet perched 'as a matter of convenience on the top of her head' — that one clause does everything.
It tells you who Mrs Boffin is: practical, unsentimental about appearances, entirely unconcerned with propriety.
And then that bonnet becomes the instrument of violence — old Harmon snatching it, sending it spinning.
The comedy of the detail and the brutality of what follows — Dickens holds those two things together without flinching.
And this is the inheritance young John carries — not money, but the knowledge that these two people suffered for him when he was powerless.
The legal context sharpens that suffering considerably.
Old Harmon's tyranny over his household was not merely personal — it was structural. Domestic servants had virtually no legal recourse against an employer's violence.
And the boy himself — disinherited by temperament, dependent on a father's whim — existed in a kind of legal limbo throughout his youth.
This is why the Dutch bottle matters so enormously when we reach the climactic confrontation with Wegg.
A will of more recent date than the one Boffin proved — and Harmon reveals it with extraordinary controlled fury.

'It is a will of my late father's, of more recent date than the will proved by Mr Boffin (address whom again, as you have addressed him already, and I'll knock you down), leaving the whole of his property to the Crown.'
The parenthetical threat — issued mid-legal-declaration — is Dickens at his most bracingly comic.
What interests me in that confrontation is the moral geometry Dickens constructs around Boffin.
Harmon tells us that Boffin buried the Dutch bottle in the Mound — not to defraud, but because the document cast a slur on the memory of children who had done nothing to deserve it.
The passage makes this precise, and it is worth dwelling on.

'That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.'
'My unhappy self-tormenting father' — that phrase is doing immense work.
It is not hatred. It is not forgiveness. It is something colder and more adult: a diagnosis.
And then there is the sister. 'Then already dead of a broken heart.'
She appears in the novel as a kind of ghost — barely present, never named in her own voice — and yet that parenthesis suddenly gives her weight.
A broken heart. As cause of death. In a legal document about inheritance.
Dickens buries the most devastating emotional fact in what looks like a subordinate clause, and the effect is almost unbearable.
The violence in the Wegg confrontation is worth pausing over, because it is quite deliberate — and Harmon makes no apology for it.
Harmon has just knocked Wegg's head against the wall and announces cheerfully that he'd welcome the opportunity to do worse.
'I mean to knock your head against the wall, and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out. Listen, you scoundrel, and look at that Dutch bottle.'
What's revealing here is the specific sum: a thousand pounds.
It is a wealthy man's fantasy of retribution, expressed with the exactitude of a man who now controls great property.
Justice and vengeance wear the same face, and Dickens doesn't particularly try to pry them apart.
There is also something to be said for the surveillance plot — the way Harmon and Sloppy have watched Wegg throughout.
Harmon explains the mechanism with a certain relish that I think tells us something about the character's deeper temperament.
'I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.'
Harmon has been conducting a parallel deception to his own disguise — watching the watcher.
One might argue this is not entirely admirable — prolonging a deception 'to the last possible moment' so that Wegg's disappointment should be maximum.
That is retribution calculated by the minute. There is something almost — Old Testament about it.
And then Dickens does something I find genuinely startling — he steps forward himself, in his own voice, in a postscript.
He addresses those readers who thought he was trying to conceal the Harmon-Rokesmith identity, and he gently but firmly defends his craft.

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
What a quietly combative sentence that is.
He is not apologising for the ambiguity — he is claiming it as the point.
The artist, he says, may perhaps be trusted to know what he is about — if we'll concede him a little patience.
And having lived with this novel for thirty years, I think he earned that patience.
What that authorial intrusion also does, legally speaking, is remind us how high the stakes of serial publication were.
Readers were speculating month by month, debating plot points in periodicals — and Dickens was writing under that pressure.
The remark about trusting an artist to know his vocation is also, I suspect, a retort to specific critics in the weekly press.
We've moved from a bonnet spinning across a yard to a will buried in a mound of dust — and both images carry the same weight: the past refusing to stay buried.
John Harmon's shadow falls across every part of this novel — even, it turns out, across the author's own relationship with his readers.
We'll continue in our next segment, where we turn to the world Harmon re-enters — and what it costs to come back from the dead.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been talking about the novel's grand architecture — the dust mounds, the river, the inheritance — but this segment turns to something equally Dickensian: the comedy of corruption.
Because Dickens doesn't just indict the villains of this novel — he makes them absurd.
And Caroline Woodcourt, our close reader, has been living in exactly those passages — the ones where the laugh and the shudder arrive together.
Caroline, where shall we begin?
I want to begin with Silas Wegg, because Wegg is one of the great comic villains in English fiction, and I think he's sometimes underestimated.
He's not just scheming — he's grandiose about his scheming.
There's a passage where Wegg lays out his blackmail plan for Mr Venus, and the prose itself becomes a parody of legal oration.
He keeps referring to Venus as his 'comrade, brother, and partner' — every. single. time.
And then comes the plan — and the plan is breathtaking in its audacity.

He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' — and that he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.
'Abject moral bondage and slavery' — for Nicodemus Boffin, the Golden Dustman.
Dickens is laughing, but he is also completely serious about the ugliness of what Wegg represents.
What strikes me about that passage is the rhetorical inflation — the deliberate mismatch between the grandeur of the diction and the meanness of the purpose.
Wegg speaks as though he were a statesman delivering a parliamentary bill, when in fact he is a one-legged ballad-seller planning extortion.
Burke would have called it a perversion of the forms of civilised discourse — and Dickens understood exactly that perversion.
The comedy is inseparable from the moral indictment.

Notice too that Wegg himself offers a kind of parliamentary reading — he even invites amendment: 'It might be more according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths.'
The man is constitutionally incapable of simple greed — he must dress it up in procedure.
The procedural parody cuts even deeper when you consider what Wegg and Venus are actually doing: they are imitating the logic of legal extortion that operated quite openly in early Victorian England.
The suppression of a will, the leverage of a document — these were real instruments of coercion, used against heirs and inheritors with alarming frequency.
Dickens isn't inventing the mechanism — he's holding a mirror to it, but fitting the mirror with a grotesque frame.
And the Deputy Lock scene makes the same point from below — from the institutional petty corruption of someone at the very bottom of the patronage chain.
There's a man who takes Betty Higden's coins — pocketing them one by one — and simultaneously announces his virtue.

'I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow' — and here he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous industry.
The gesture — wiping the brow after pocketing stolen coins — that is Dickens at his most surgical.
That wiping of the sleeve is one of those Dickens stage directions that you cannot shake.
You see the man performing his own virtue for an audience of one — for Betty Higden, who has nothing.
And then — 'Go where you like.' The dismissal is total.
But then there's the Wegg keyhole scene, which operates differently — it's more purely theatrical, almost like a pantomime.
Listen to this — the image Dickens gives us of Wegg and Boffin is almost surreal.
Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.
'An imaginary grindstone.' The cruelty is mimed — and Boffin is made to stoop at a keyhole to a torture that isn't even real.
And Wegg laughs silently — which is somehow far worse than laughing aloud.
The silent laugh is a superb detail — and entirely characteristic of Dickens's understanding that the deepest contempt is silent.
Wegg has reduced Boffin — the Golden Dustman, the man of property — to a figure stooping at a keyhole.
It is a comic image, but it is also a moral image — a man humiliated by another man's baseness.
Dickens understood that comedy and shame can occupy the same moment — indeed, that is where his greatest effects live.
And there's another layer to all of this — which is the identity question running beneath the comedy.
John Harmon moves through this novel wearing multiple faces — Rokesmith, Handford — and the prose itself captures that multiplicity with an almost vertiginous precision.
The scene where he stows the false hair and whisker in his coat and becomes simultaneously three men — that's not just a plot device.
It's a comment on how Victorian society constructed identity — through appearance, through documentation, through the signatures in ledgers.
That passage is extraordinary to read aloud — the syntax itself keeps folding back on itself.
Dickens gives us this formulation that he repeats — and the repetition is the point.
'Became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world.'
And then — almost immediately — the same sentence returns: 'For John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world.'
Three men, one body — and each one absolutely, impossibly like the other.
It's comic and it's gothic at the same time, and that phrase 'never man was like another in this world' keeps tolling like a bell.
The laugh and the shudder — and the bell tolling underneath both of them.
That feels like the essence of what we've been circling today — a novelist who refuses to let comedy and darkness occupy separate rooms.
Thank you to Caroline, to Edmund, and to James for a conversation that has made me want to go back and re-read every one of these passages immediately.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.
Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we're turning our attention to one of Dickens's most richly drawn character arcs — the moral education of Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a young woman who is frankly, cheerfully, almost defiantly mercenary about money.
And yet by the end she has become something quite different — and the novel makes us feel every step of that transformation.
With me today are three readers who've thought very deeply about this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a literary traditionalist — he'll be asking what kind of moral imagination is actually at work here.
Professor James Blackstone, our social historian, will root us in the real world of Victorian poverty and institutional life that surrounds Bella's story.
And Caroline Woodcourt, our close reader, will keep us honest about what it actually feels like to read these passages — sentence by sentence.
Edmund, let me start with you. Bella's transformation is often described as a moral one — but is it really? Or is it something more complicated than that?
It is, I think, genuinely moral — but one must resist the temptation to flatten it into mere didacticism.
What Dickens gives us in Bella is not a lesson delivered from without, but a conscience discovering itself from within.
There is a scene — quite wonderful — where Bella retires to her room after an evening with the Boffins and finds herself deeply unsettled.
She addresses herself in the looking-glass, which is a marvellous conceit, and demands:

'Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
Now that is not a young woman receiving a moral lesson. That is a young woman conducting a moral cross-examination of herself.
The looking-glass is the instrument of vanity, yes — but here it becomes the instrument of conscience. Dickens inverts the symbol with great economy.
Burke would have called it the operations of natural moral sentiment — and I think he would have been right.
And what makes it sting — quite literally sting — is that Bella knows she is being inconsistent and cannot quite stop herself.
The word 'Beast' — directed at herself — is almost shocking. It's one of those moments where you stop and read the sentence twice.
It's funny, yes — there's a comic register — but it's also genuinely painful. She sees herself clearly and doesn't like what she sees.
And what's so clever is that Dickens doesn't let us feel superior to her. We understand exactly why she feels what she feels.
I'd like to bring in the context that surrounds Bella's transformation, because I think it matters enormously who she is being changed by and what she is being changed in relation to.
Rokesmith — who is of course John Harmon in disguise — is staging a kind of social experiment on her.
He tells us himself, in that long retrospective confession, exactly what he intended.
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving' her. He uses the word deliberately, as if she is a theorem, or a substance being tested in a laboratory.
Now, one can read that generously — as a man desperate not to repeat the degradation his father's money had already caused.
But one can also read it as a rather cold-blooded act of surveillance, which puts Bella in the position of a subject, not a partner.
That is a perfectly legitimate reading, Professor Blackstone, and I confess Harmon's scheme sits rather uncomfortably with me too.
But I would distinguish between the moral quality of an action and the moral significance of its consequences.
Harmon's deception may be discomfiting. The conscience it stirs in Bella is nonetheless entirely her own.
Dickens is, after all, showing us a character capable of genuine growth. That capacity comes from within her, whatever the external stimulus.
Can I draw in another thread here? Because Bella's moral education doesn't happen in isolation. It happens in proximity to people whose lives are genuinely hard.
There's a passage I keep returning to — Lizzie Hexam describing a little girl who has grown up surrounded by drunkenness and ruin.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthesis — 'if she ever had one' — is devastating. Lizzie doesn't labour the point. She just lets it fall.
And the effect, I think, is to put Bella's situation — her complaint that she is a poor girl who wants nice things — into a very different light.
She has the luxury of being inconsistent. This child doesn't have that luxury.
That contrast is doing a great deal of moral work in the novel, and I think it's intentional rather than incidental.
The girl Lizzie describes has a father who is — and this detail is crucial — a good workman, but destroyed by drink.
That is not a moral failing presented as simple wickedness. That is a portrait of systemic ruin — poverty and alcohol and the absence of any support structure.
And then you place Bella, warm and charming and frankly a little spoilt, against that backdrop. The effect is not to condemn Bella. It is to educate her — and us.
What's also worth noting is that Dickens handles charitable institutions with absolutely withering contempt in the same stretch of the novel.
Mr Boffin's tirade about charity patronage lists is one of the funniest things in the book — but the anger underneath it is real.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
That cascade of titles — each one more absurd than the last — is the sound of self-congratulation institutionalised.
Boffin is magnificent in that passage. And one notes that the outrage is delivered not by a reformer or an intellectual, but by a man of plain common sense.
Dickens distrusts institutions almost as much as Dr. Johnson distrusted abstractions. The indictment comes from lived decency, not from theory.

And that, I would argue, is precisely the moral grammar of Bella's transformation as well. She does not arrive at goodness by reasoning her way to it. She arrives through feeling — through contact with people who matter.
And that contact is so beautifully rendered in the scene with Lizzie. There's a moment between them — late in Book Three — where Lizzie confesses her feelings about Eugene Wrayburn.
She says something that I find almost unbearably poignant about the way she holds love that she knows she cannot act on.
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
'The light of them' — meaning his eyes. She will not look at him again. But she needs that light to remain somewhere in the world.
And she is telling this to Bella. That intimacy — that moment of absolute trust offered to a young woman who began the novel caring primarily for herself — is part of Bella's education too.
It seems to me that Bella becomes worthy of that trust — and the novel lets us watch her grow into it.
There's one further image I want to place alongside all of this, because I think it crystallises what Dickens is doing with Bella's arc.
Rokesmith — still in his disguise — watches Bella from a doorway as Betty Higden takes her leave. And Dickens writes:

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
'Away from paralysis and pauperism.' Betty Higden would rather die in a ditch than enter the workhouse. That is the world Bella is being asked to see.
And Rokesmith — standing in that doorway, watching — is not merely watching Bella. He is watching whether she sees.
That image of the doorway is wonderfully suggestive — the watcher watched, the test conducted in plain sight.
We've been talking about gold and grace, and I think what's emerged is that Dickens refuses to separate them — the money question and the moral question are the same question for Bella.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the river — that other great moral landscape in this novel — and ask what it means that so much of the plot turns on what is pulled from its depths.

segments.title: The Weight of Inheritance: Character and Circumstance

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — slowly, carefully, with enormous pleasure.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about inheritance — about what money does to people, what it reveals about them, what it corrupts.
And today's segment goes to the very heart of that: the Boffins, the dust heaps, and the swarm of humanity that descends when wealth becomes public knowledge.
With me today are three readers who know this novel with something close to intimacy.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that the novel's great subject is individual moral character — not social programme.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — the law, the institutions, the real texture of Victorian poverty and philanthropy.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it, she tells me, for the prose as much as the story.
Let's begin with the Boffins — newly enriched, suddenly famous, immediately besieged.
The passage that introduces Boffin in his mansion is one of the most beautifully precise comic images Dickens ever produced.
He sets up the comparison with absolute confidence —
"like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites."
A cheese. An aristocratic family cheese.
The image is absurd, but it is also exact — because the mansion does breed parasites, and we are about to meet them in their hundreds.
And Boffin just — accepts it all. He regards it as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty.
What strikes me there is the word 'content.'
Dickens tells us Boffin is content because Mrs Boffin is delighted and Bella is delighted — not because the mansion pleases him.
That is a very careful moral portrait: a man whose happiness is entirely located in the happiness of others.
Whether that goodness survives what the novel puts him through is, of course, the question the book is asking.
And what the novel puts him through, almost immediately, is the full machinery of Victorian charitable extraction.
The Secretary's inventory of solicitations is extraordinary documentary evidence, as well as brilliant comedy.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, twenty-seven organs — Dickens is cataloguing a real phenomenon.
The moment a name was publicly associated with new money in Victorian England, a very organised industry mobilised.
And the Duke of Linseed's letter is the masterpiece of that section —
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words of physical description that annihilate three pages of pompous solicitation before we've even read a word of it.
And the postscript! 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — Dickens calls it 'thoughtful in the postscript.'
That single word 'thoughtful' does all the work — the irony is so controlled it barely raises its voice.
And then we learn it's lithographed by the hundred — a personalised appeal that is not personal at all.
That gap between performance and reality is what the whole novel is about, really.
The individual beggars in the following passage are even more interesting to me as studies in human nature.
Dickens anatomises each type with clinical precision, but there is something underneath the comedy — a genuine pathos.
The observation about the documents is devastating in its accuracy —
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
What a comparison. Grotesque, precise, and — if you think about it for a moment — deeply sad.
The categorisation of beggars here is almost sociological — the daughters of general officers, the inspired beggars, the nobly independent beggars.
Each category corresponds to a genuinely recognisable Victorian social type — Dickens is not inventing these people, he is classifying them.
The 'nobly independent' beggars who want a loan at five per cent per annum — that is a real Victorian species: the gentleman-debtor who reframes begging as a financial transaction.
What Dickens understands is that poverty has its own taxonomy — its own elaborate fictions about itself.
The beggars who will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday — I find that genuinely chilling, even inside the comedy.
Because 'cold in death' is such a theatrical phrase — and Dickens lets it stand there, ludicrous and terrible at once.
The desperation underneath all these performances is real, even if the performances themselves are absurd.
And then there is the other side of that equation — not the beggars looking in from outside, but the predators already inside the house.
Because Silas Wegg is something rather more dangerous than a petitioner. Edmund, would you take us to that passage?
Wegg is Dickens's most precise study in what we might call the psychology of petty resentment elevated to malice.
The narrator's observation here is one of those sentences that stops you cold —
"Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures."
That is not satirical. That is Dickens stating, with complete conviction, a truth about human character.
And what makes it so shrewd is the parenthesis — 'unless it be the power of intellect or virtue.'
He is not saying power corrupts in some general Acton-ish sense. He is saying that only base natures are attracted to power for its own sake.
The image of stripping the roof off like a house of cards is also doing important work there.
Wegg's power is entirely destructive — he cannot build anything, he can only threaten to demolish.
And this connects to the will that Wegg believes he has found — the document that he thinks reorders everything.
The language he uses to describe it is revealing — he reads it out with the self-importance of a man who has finally, in his own mind, become consequential.
And the will itself is a masterpiece of bitter clarity —

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Quite enough for him.' That phrase is brutal — the testator's contempt carried intact into the grave.
And what Wegg hears in that will, of course, is an opportunity — not justice, not truth, but leverage.
He is, in that moment, exactly the same creature as all those beggars the Secretary is sorting through — except he thinks he has found a document that is actually a document.
The whole novel keeps returning to this: what do we think we are owed, and what would we do to collect it?
That is precisely the novel's moral architecture, as I read it.
Every character in this book is placed in a situation where they must decide what they will do when circumstance offers them a choice between decency and advantage.
Boffin accepts the parasites with resignation and good humour. Wegg circles the house like a vulture, drunk on the idea of power.
That contrast is not social satire — it is a moral argument.
Inheritance, then, as a kind of test — and the novel is quietly, relentlessly marking the papers.
We'll return after the break to follow the money a little further — and to ask what it does, in the end, to those who are given it and those who simply want it.

segments.title: Reading Between the Lines: Dickens's Narrative Games

utterances.text: Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we turn our attention to Dickens's narrative craft itself.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel full of disguises, false identities, and information withheld — both from characters and from us as readers.
Dickens is playing games with us, and today we want to ask: how does he do it, and why does it work so beautifully?
Edmund Leigh has been looking closely at some of the novel's most carefully constructed moments of revelation — and misdirection.
Edmund, where would you like to begin?
I would begin, if I may, with what I consider one of the most audacious pieces of narrative sleight of hand in the entire novel.
Riderhood — that magnificently degraded creature — makes his accusation against Gaffer Hexam with a solemnity that is almost liturgical.
Dickens gives the speech a particular repetitive weight — listen to how it is phrased.
'I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.'
'The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.'
That tripling of the phrase — 'the hand,' 'the hand,' 'his hand' — has the cadence of an oath sworn before God.
And the reader, at this moment, is entirely inclined to believe it.
But the reversal that follows is — I think — even more remarkable.
Riderhood has built his whole accusation — his whole moral standing in that scene — on certainty.
And then the body is pulled from the river and it is Gaffer himself.
Riderhood's response is only four words, and they are a masterpiece of involuntary self-exposure.
'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'
Not grief. Not shock. The first instinct is betrayal — of himself.
Dickens convicts a man with his own exclamation. That is character revealed under pressure — which is, I would argue, the highest art of fiction.
What strikes me about both those moments is how much Dickens trusts the reader's ear.
He doesn't tell us that Riderhood is performing his certainty — he makes us hear the performance.
And then 'Gaffer's done me' — that little phrase — collapses the whole edifice in an instant.
There is no other novelist, I think, who can end a scene with quite that economy.
I think we should also notice the institutional setting of Riderhood's accusation — he is making a formal deposition before officers.
The phrase 'let me be took down again' is enormously revealing — this is a man who knows how the machinery of official accusation works.
He is exploiting the law's appetite for named perpetrators and clean narratives.
The irony that the law then produces Gaffer's body from the very river that was supposed to incriminate him — that is Dickens at his most sardonic about official process.
Quite so. And the same machinery of hidden knowledge operates at a far more sustained level with John Harmon's disguise.
When Dickens finally lets Harmon narrate his own scheme, the confession reads almost like a man checking his memory against the record.
He even pauses to verify his own account — in a manner that is quietly extraordinary for a Victorian narrator.
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
And then — with wonderful strangeness — he says: 'I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right.'
A man interrogating his own reliability as a narrator. Dickens is decades ahead of his time.
That self-questioning — 'I have all these facts right? Yes' — is one of my favourite moments in the whole novel.
Because it sounds so sane, so methodical — and yet it comes from a man who has been living as a ghost of himself.
What Dickens is doing, I think, is showing us how identity itself becomes provisional when you choose to disappear.
You have to reconstruct even your own past in the third person to be sure it was real.
There is a legal dimension to that too, which I find compelling.
Harmon has, in the eyes of the law, inherited a fortune and then — apparently — died.
His scheme with Radfoot is not just romantic impulsiveness — it is a deliberate suspension of his legal personhood.
He steps outside the machinery of property and identity that the whole novel is built around — and watches it run without him.
And the reward for that self-erasure is not fortune — it is something Dickens prizes far more.
There is a passage late in the novel — a supper scene — that I find more affecting than almost anything else in the book.
Bella and Rokesmith — and old Wilfer — sharing a meal in a poky office, surrounded by the brass knobs of a commercial safe.
Dickens reaches for a fairy-tale register, and then immediately undercuts it — and yet the joy survives the undercutting.

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'

'The uncongenial oddity of its surroundings, with the two brass knobs of the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring from a corner, like the eyes of some dull dragon, only made it the more delightful.'
That 'only made it the more delightful' — the adversative turned into an intensifier — is Dickens's deepest moral argument, made through comedy.
Poverty does not corrupt joy. It can, under the right conditions of character, concentrate it.
The 'dull dragon' is such a perfect detail — those staring brass knobs domesticated into a fairy-tale monster.
It's exactly the kind of sentence you stop and read twice — once for the laugh, and once to ask how he did it.
And the fact that old R. Wilfer is there — the gentle, defeated father — adds a tenderness that lifts the whole scene.
It's remarkable how Dickens can move from the gothic menace of the river to a fairy-tale supper in a counting-house, and have both feel entirely true.
That tonal range — and the narrative intelligence that controls it — is precisely what makes this novel so endlessly rewarding to read.
We'll be back shortly to look more closely at the novel's world of money, dust, and the strange alchemy of inheritance.
We've spent this episode tracing the novel's great circulations — of money, of identity, of moral weight.
And perhaps no arc in the book asks us to feel all of that more acutely than Bella Wilfer's.
She begins the novel as a self-declared worshipper of money — frank about it, almost proud.
And then Dickens places her inside the Boffin household, and things become considerably more complicated.
Caroline, you've re-read this novel more times than most people have read it once — what does Bella's transformation feel like from the inside of the reading experience?
It feels like being watched — and watching yourself being watched.
There's a moment in Chapter 38 that I keep returning to, where Bella steals a glance at Mr Boffin.
"A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face."
That word — once — does so much quiet damage.
It means Bella remembers who Boffin was, which means she can measure what he is becoming.
And because she is also changing, she is watching a mirror she would very much prefer not to look into.
That's beautifully put, and I think it identifies what is genuinely remarkable about these chapters.
Boffin's corruption — or what presents itself as corruption — is rendered in the grammar of a sermon.
Listen to him advise Bella.
"Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich."
The repetition of the word money is not accidental — it's a liturgy, an incantation.
And the unctuous manner Dickens specifies — that rolling, relishing R-r-rich — is a performance of greed, not greed itself.
Which raises the question — and the novel will answer it — of who is performing for whom.
The social context here is worth holding onto, because Boffin's advice is not absurd — it is, by Victorian standards, rational.
A young woman of Bella's class had almost no legal or economic agency of her own.
Marriage was the mechanism by which she either secured or surrendered her economic fate.
What makes Bella's arc so pointed is that she understands this perfectly — she's not naive.
And yet the novel refuses to let that understanding be a sufficient excuse.
When she encounters Lizzie Hexam's selfless devotion, the novel engineers a very funny and very precise act of self-reckoning.
"There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?"
And she gives herself a penitential poke in the side.
That poke in the side is one of the most purely Dickensian gestures in the whole novel.
It's comic, and it's entirely real.
Bella cannot quite articulate her shame to anyone, so she lodges it physically in herself.
The body registers what the conscious mind has not yet been willing to admit.
That's how Dickens marks moral turning points — not with speeches, but with gestures.
And that is precisely where I would push back against readings that reduce Bella to a social type.
She is not merely a product of her economic circumstances.
The poke in the side is an act of moral will — small, ridiculous, and entirely genuine.
It is the beginning of what Dr. Johnson would have called the amendment of the will.
Dickens believes in that process — laboriously, painfully, sometimes comically — and so does his novel.
I wouldn't disagree — only to add that the novel is honest about the cost.
That dark cloud over Boffin's face — the suspicion, covetousness, conceit — Bella has to sit with that.
She has to watch someone she has come to love apparently diminish, and wonder if she has somehow contributed to it.
The moral education in this novel is not comfortable, and it doesn't pretend to be.
Bella Wilfer — vain, funny, self-aware, and finally willing to poke herself into a better self.
There may be no more honest portrait of moral growth in the Victorian novel than that.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done full justice to this extraordinary book.
Our Mutual Friend repays every reading — and I hope today has sent you back to its pages.
Until next time.

It being Lizzie’s regular occupation when they were alone of an evening to

c44:p10.text:
The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended
      nearer to the floor outside the outer door of the chambers. The doors of
      the rooms within, appeared to be standing open. There were rays of
      candlelight from one of them, and there was the sound of a footstep going
      about. There were two voices. The words they uttered were not
      distinguishable, but they were both the voices of men. In a few moments
      the voices were silent, and there was no sound of footstep, and the inner
      light went out. If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him
      awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke
      of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of
      the night.

c52:p102.text:
She passed out and he followed her. Mr and Mrs Boffin had the curiosity
      softly to raise a window and look after them as they went down the long
      street. They walked arm-in-arm, showily enough, but without appearing to
      interchange a syllable. It might have been fanciful to suppose that under
      their outer bearing there was something of the shamed air of two cheats
      who were linked together by concealed handcuffs; but, not so, to suppose
      that they were haggardly weary of one another, of themselves, and of all
      this world. In turning the street corner they might have turned out of
      this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the
      contrary; for, they set eyes on the Lammles never more.
c52:p102.summary: The Lammles depart arm-in-arm but in silence and spiritual wretchedness, walking with all the appearance of propriety but no genuine connection, and are never seen again—Dickens' final judgment on their morally empty lives.
c52:p102.best_quote: In turning the street corner they might have turned out of this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the contrary

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’
c8:p39.summary: Boffin details how he and Mrs Boffin repeatedly defended young John Harmon against Old Harmon's cruelty, including an incident where Harmon struck Mrs Boffin and she collapsed, establishing their selfless advocacy for the boy.
c8:p39.best_quote: I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard... and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.

c64:p97.text:
‘That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills
      made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything
      absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and
      reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.
      That Dutch bottle was found by my noble benefactor and yours, after he
      entered on possession of the estate. That Dutch bottle distressed him
      beyond measure, because, though I and my sister were both no more, it cast
      a slur upon our memory which he knew we had done nothing in our miserable
      youth, to deserve. That Dutch bottle, therefore, he buried in the Mound
      belonging to him, and there it lay while you, you thankless wretch, were
      prodding and poking—often very near it, I dare say. His intention
      was, that it should never see the light; but he was afraid to destroy it,
      lest to destroy such a document, even with his great generous motive,
      might be an offence at law. After the discovery was made here who I was,
      Mr Boffin, still restless on the subject, told me, upon certain conditions
      impossible for such a hound as you to appreciate, the secret of that Dutch
      bottle. I urged upon him the necessity of its being dug up, and the paper
      being legally produced and established. The first thing you saw him do,
      and the second thing has been done without your knowledge. Consequently,
      the paper now rattling in your hand as I shake you—and I should like
      to shake the life out of you—is worth less than the rotten cork of
      the Dutch bottle, do you understand?’
c64:p97.summary: Harmon explains how the Dutch bottle was found by Boffin after entering the estate, buried in the Mound to hide its contents, and later exhumed without Wegg's knowledge.
c64:p97.best_quote: That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.

c64:p89.text:
‘It is a will of my late father’s, of more recent date than the will
      proved by Mr Boffin (address whom again, as you have addressed him
      already, and I’ll knock you down), leaving the whole of his property to
      the Crown,’ said John Harmon, with as much indifference as was compatible
      with extreme sternness.
c64:p89.summary: Harmon reveals that the Dutch bottle contains a will leaving everything to the Crown, making Wegg's document worthless.
c64:p89.best_quote: It is a will of my late father's, of more recent date than the will proved by Mr Boffin (address whom again, as you have addressed him already, and I'll knock you down), leaving the whole of his property to the Crown.

c64:p95.text:
‘I mean to knock your head against the wall,’ returned John Harmon,
      suiting his action to his words, with the heartiest good will; ‘and I’d
      give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out. Listen, you
      scoundrel, and look at that Dutch bottle.’
c64:p95.summary: Harmon violently interrogates Wegg while ordering Sloppy to hold up the Dutch bottle, explaining its significance and his own indebtedness to Boffin.
c64:p95.best_quote: and I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out.

c64:p99.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p99.summary: Harmon explains that they discovered Wegg's find through Venus, watched him closely, and deliberately prolonged his deception to maximize his disappointment.
c64:p99.best_quote: I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
c40:p72.summary: Wegg proposes an elaborate scheme: let Boffin excavate the Mounds at his own expense while they observe, then when the work is done, threaten him with the earlier will and extort half his property. If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.
c40:p72.best_quote: That, he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' ... he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.

c30:p3.text:
Here he ceased to be the oakum-headed, oakum-whiskered man on whom Miss
      Pleasant Riderhood had looked, and, allowing for his being still wrapped
      in a nautical overcoat, became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius
      Handford, as never man was like another in this world. In the breast of
      the coat he stowed the bristling hair and whisker, in a moment, as the
      favouring wind went with him down a solitary place that it had swept clear
      of passengers. Yet in that same moment he was the Secretary also, Mr
      Boffin’s Secretary. For John Rokesmith, too, was as like that same lost
      wanted Mr Julius Handford as never man was like another in this world.
c30:p3.summary: The oakum-headed disguised man removes his false hair and whisker, revealing himself to be John Harmon, who is also the Secretary John Rokesmith, all three identities being the same lost and wanted Julius Handford.
c30:p3.best_quote: became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world

c38:p55.text:
Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity
      that dates from my childhood with my poor sister.

‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am
      not sorry. I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a
      moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.’

c25:p0.text:
The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic
      family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite
      amount of parasites; but he was content to regard this drawback on his
      property as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty. He felt the more resigned to
      it, forasmuch as Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was
      delighted.
c25:p0.summary: Nicodemus Boffin, the newly wealthy Golden Dustman, has settled into his grand mansion, finding it oversized but content because Mrs Boffin and Bella are delighted.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c40:p97.text:
For, Silas Wegg felt it to be quite out of the question that he could lay
      his head upon his pillow in peace, without first hovering over Mr Boffin’s
      house in the superior character of its Evil Genius. Power (unless it be
      the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the
      lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with
      his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a
      house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.

      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense

      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at

      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to

      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.

c38:p47.text:
‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an
      unctuous manner. ‘R—r—rich!’
